milestones.title: Dutch settlement of New Amsterdam
milestones.detail: Dutch West India Company colonists settle at the mouth of the Hudson; in 1625 the southern tip of Manhattan is chosen for Fort Amsterdam and the settlement becomes the capital of New Netherland.

milestones.title: New Amsterdam receives municipal rights
milestones.detail: The settlement formally becomes a city on 2 February 1653.

milestones.title: English takeover; renamed New York
milestones.detail: The city comes under English control in 1664 and is renamed New York after the Duke of York; about 2,500 people live there.

milestones.title: British occupation and the Great Fire
milestones.detail: British forces occupy the city in 1776 and hold it until late 1783. A fire on 20-21 September 1776 destroys between 10 and 25 percent of its buildings.

milestones.title: Capital of the United States
milestones.detail: The Congress of the Confederation makes New York the national capital in January 1785; it remains so until 1790.

milestones.title: Commissioners' Plan lays out the street grid
milestones.detail: The city adopts the Commissioners' Plan of 1811, extending a regular street grid over almost all of Manhattan.

milestones.title: Erie Canal opens
milestones.detail: The canal connects the Atlantic port, via the Hudson, to the Great Lakes and the agricultural interior; by 1835 New York is the largest city in the United States.

milestones.title: Great Fire of 1835
milestones.detail: A fire in the middle of an economic boom covers 17 city blocks in Lower Manhattan and destroys hundreds of buildings.

milestones.title: Croton Aqueduct brings clean water
milestones.detail: Built between 1837 and 1842, the aqueduct carries water 41 miles from the Croton River to reservoirs in Manhattan.

milestones.title: Central Park opens
milestones.detail: Olmsted and Vaux win the design competition in 1858 and the park's first areas open to the public late that year; it is completed in 1876.

milestones.title: Brooklyn Bridge opens
milestones.detail: The bridge between Manhattan and Brooklyn opens on 24 May 1883 after 14 years of construction.

milestones.title: Ellis Island immigration station opens
milestones.detail: From 1892 to 1954 about 12 million immigrants arriving at the port are processed on Ellis Island.

milestones.title: Five boroughs consolidated
milestones.detail: On 1 January 1898 Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island are consolidated into the City of Greater New York.

milestones.title: Subway opens
milestones.detail: The New York City Subway opens on 27 October 1904 and helps bind the consolidated city together.

milestones.title: Empire State Building completed
milestones.detail: At 381 m the Empire State Building overtakes the Chrysler Building (318.9 m, 1930) as the tallest building in the city.

milestones.title: September 11 attacks
milestones.detail: Hijacked airliners destroy the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center on 11 September 2001; the attacks kill 2,977 people.

milestones.title: Hurricane Sandy
milestones.detail: Hurricane Sandy hits the city hard in October 2012; at least 43 people die in New York City and economic losses there are estimated at $19 billion.

notes: Start date: sources differ between 1624 (first Dutch West India Company colonists; the settlement date given in the New Amsterdam and New York City articles), 1625 (Fort Amsterdam sited on Manhattan; the settlement made capital of New Netherland) and 1626 (the settlement named New Amsterdam). 1624 is used. No population figure was found for 1624-1663; the first point is an estimate of 2,500 for 1664. Population definitions: 1698-1771 are colonial censuses of New York County (Manhattan); 1790-1870 are federal censuses of New York City when it was Manhattan only; 1880 and 1890 include the part of the Bronx annexed in 1874; from 1900 the figures are for the consolidated five boroughs, so the rise from 1,515,301 (1890) to 3,437,202 (1900) is mostly a boundary change (the 1898 consolidation added Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island and the rest of the Bronx). These are city-proper counts, whereas the UN series from 1950 covers the wider urban agglomeration, so expect a step up at 1950. Chandler's agglomeration estimates for comparison are 1,900,000 (1875), 4,242,000 (1900) and 7,774,000 (1925). Census figures were read from the Wikipedia demographics table, which cites the Census Bureau working paper; the working paper itself was not opened. Landmarks: skyscraper heights and years are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center (demolished towers from their individual CTBUH pages; coordinates of demolished buildings from Wikipedia). Bridge heights are tower heights. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Fort Amsterdam, St. Paul's Chapel (1766), Federal Hall, Castle Clinton, Grand Central Terminal.
